checkpoints.title: Find anomalies and trace a single request
checkpoints.prompt: An operations person for the Orders API investigates, for one slow request, whether the Inventory Service or the Payment Service took more time. Choose the most appropriate data to use.

choices.text: The Orders API’s average response time over one hour
choices.explanation: An aggregate value cannot show how much time each service took for one specific request.

choices.text: The target request’s trace and the time taken by each call
choices.explanation: A trace records the time for each processing step along the path of one request.

choices.text: One log line from when the Orders API started
choices.explanation: A startup record does not show the processing time for the target request.

choices.text: The name of the Orders API’s SLO
choices.explanation: The SLO name alone cannot be used to inspect individual calls.

learning.reason: A trace records the time for each processing step along the path of one request.
learning.concept: Use metrics to narrow the scope of an anomaly.

checkpoints.title: Observe response time, errors, load, and capacity
checkpoints.prompt: Users of the Orders API are waiting longer, and server processing queues are also growing. Choose two aspects the operator should examine when investigating response time and spare processing capacity.

choices.text: Saturation
choices.explanation: A growing queue may indicate that processing capacity is nearing its limit.

choices.text: Traffic volume
choices.explanation: This shows the request volume, but how much spare processing capacity remains must be investigated separately.

choices.text: Error rate
choices.explanation: The proportion of failed processing and the time until a response are separate metrics.

choices.text: Response time
choices.explanation: This measures how long users waited for a response.

learning.reason: A growing queue may indicate that processing capacity is nearing its limit. The time users waited for a response can be measured.
learning.concept: Measure the impact on users with response time and errors.

checkpoints.title: Define quality metrics and objectives
checkpoints.prompt: The operations team for the order API uses CloudWatch to determine success or failure for each request and sets an SLO targeting a success rate of at least 99.9%. Select two items needed to determine the success rate and whether the objective has been met.

choices.text: The operations included in the aggregation and which responses count as successful
choices.explanation: When the scope and success criteria are defined, other team members can calculate the success rate in the same way.

choices.text: The target value of 99.9% and the aggregation period for counting the in-scope requests.
choices.explanation: For a request-level SLO, verify which period's requests to aggregate and which target value the resulting percentage must meet.

choices.text: Only the name of the SLO to display
choices.explanation: Choosing a name does not define how quality is measured or the conditions for achieving the objective.

choices.text: Only the alert notification destination
choices.explanation: The notification destination is not a condition needed to calculate achievement.

learning.reason: When the scope and success criteria are defined, other team members can calculate the success rate in the same way. Evaluating the objective requires both the percentage and the period over which the in-scope requests are aggregated.
learning.concept: An SLI is the value being measured, while an SLO is the objective to achieve for that value.

checkpoints.title: Formulate hypotheses about causes and measure the effectiveness of countermeasures
checkpoints.prompt: After an operations engineer deploys the order API to production, the response time increases. Select the most appropriate method for determining whether this deployment caused the issue.

choices.text: Confirm the cause as soon as the response becomes slower immediately after the deployment
choices.explanation: The request volume or the state of dependencies may also have changed during the same period.

choices.text: Remove the latency metric and restore the monitoring dashboard to normal
choices.explanation: Changing the display does not shorten the user's wait time.

choices.text: Compare before and after the change under the same load and aggregation conditions, and also check the logs and traces
choices.explanation: Keeping the comparison conditions consistent helps isolate the impact of the change from other factors.

choices.text: Change the response-time objective based on a single metric
choices.explanation: Changing the objective before investigating how long the condition will persist does not reveal the cause.

learning.reason: Keeping the comparison conditions consistent helps isolate the impact of the change from other factors.
learning.concept: Test hypotheses within a narrowly defined scope.

choices.text: The number of requests per minute
choices.explanation: Plotting values measured at the same interval reveals changes in load.

choices.text: The order of services through which one order passed
choices.explanation: The path of a single request is recorded in a trace.

choices.text: An exception message produced by a request
choices.explanation: Information that records a specific event is handled as a log.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operator responsible for the order API compares graphs to determine whether the load changed between yesterday and today. Select one appropriate monitoring metric.
finalQuestions.title: Metrics used for monitoring

choices.text: The average CPU utilization of the API server
choices.explanation: CPU utilization does not show the time spent by each destination for a specific request.

choices.text: The start time and processing time for each call recorded in the request trace
choices.explanation: You can follow the target request and determine what was slow at each service.

choices.text: The response-time target set by the team
choices.explanation: A target value is a quality standard, not a record of the actual call time.

finalQuestions.prompt: The order API is slow, and an operator investigates which dependent service call took time for one order. Select one appropriate type of data.
finalQuestions.title: Identifying slow calls

choices.text: Determine the cause of all failures based only on the first log line found.
choices.explanation: A single record does not reveal the scope of the issue or other possible causes.

choices.text: Estimate the total number of requests for the entire day from one trace and end the investigation.
choices.explanation: One trace does not indicate the total number of requests.

choices.text: View the error rate by hour, then correlate the logs and traces from that time period.
choices.explanation: Use metrics to narrow the scope, then investigate the cause using individual data from the same time period.

finalQuestions.prompt: Errors are occurring intermittently in the order API. Select one appropriate procedure for narrowing down the time period of the anomaly and tracing the failed requests.
finalQuestions.title: From Anomalous Times to Logs and Traces

choices.text: Latency indicates the time taken to process a request.
choices.explanation: This metric captures the time users spend waiting.

choices.text: For errors, examine the number of failed operations and the failure rate.
choices.explanation: Both the number of failures and the failure rate are metrics for observing errors.

choices.text: For traffic, examine the volume of requests received during a given period.
choices.explanation: This helps you understand the load placed on the service.

choices.text: Saturation refers to the proportion of successful HTTP requests.
choices.explanation: Saturation indicates how close CPU or processing capacity is to its limit. Success rate is calculated separately.

finalQuestions.prompt: The operations team for an order API selected latency, errors, traffic, and saturation as monitoring items. Select one incorrect description of their respective roles.
finalQuestions.title: The Role of the Four Perspectives

choices.text: Conclude that the increase in CPU utilization is the cause and do not check any other metrics.
choices.explanation: An increase in request volume or another factor may have caused both.

choices.text: Check the number of requests during the same period and latency by operation.
choices.explanation: This allows you to check changes in load and the operations that were affected.

choices.text: Use logs and traces to investigate errors or timeouts in dependencies.
choices.explanation: This provides information for determining whether another cause exists.

finalQuestions.prompt: During the day, the order API showed simultaneous increases in CPU utilization and the number of HTTP 5xx errors. Select one incorrect initial response for investigating the cause.
finalQuestions.title: The Relationship Between CPU Utilization and Errors

choices.text: Conclude that there are no slow requests because the average response time has not changed
choices.explanation: Some substantial delays may not be visible from the average alone.

choices.text: Compare the p95 response times over aggregation periods of the same length for the same API operation
choices.explanation: Using the same comparison conditions makes it possible to track changes in the slower requests.

choices.text: Estimate the response time from CPU utilization and do not measure the actual response time
choices.explanation: Internal resource utilization alone cannot identify how long users waited.

choices.text: Directly compare p95 values for different operations or aggregation periods
choices.explanation: Differences in comparison conditions may appear to be differences in the values.

choices.text: Also check the number of requests and the number of items waiting for processing during the same time period
choices.explanation: This helps determine whether load or processing capacity could be a cause.

finalQuestions.prompt: The average response time for the order API is about the same as last week, but some users have reported that it is slow. Choose two ways for the person in charge to investigate the impact and cause.
finalQuestions.title: Analyzing Some Slow Requests

choices.text: The numerator is the number of target requests that succeeded within 500 milliseconds
choices.explanation: The numerator includes the number of requests that met the condition for being counted as successful.

choices.text: The denominator is the total number of requests that reached the operation being measured
choices.explanation: The denominator is the entire target population, including both successes and failures.

choices.text: A denominator is unnecessary; the proportion can be calculated from the number of successful requests alone
choices.explanation: A total number to compare against is required to calculate a proportion.

finalQuestions.prompt: The order API operations team uses the proportion of requests that succeeded within 500 milliseconds as the SLI. Choose two correct elements of the calculation.
finalQuestions.title: Order API Success Rate

choices.text: Investigate whether no order requests arrived or the measurement process stopped
choices.explanation: Either situation could result in metrics not being retrievable.

choices.text: Treat the period when metrics cannot be retrieved as normal and do not check the cause
choices.explanation: If measurement has stopped, this approach will leave the problem unnoticed.

choices.text: Check the number of requests aggregated through another path and the operating status of the measurement process
choices.explanation: Separating the observation paths makes it possible to distinguish between a state in which there are no requests and a state in which measurement has stopped.

finalQuestions.prompt: A person monitoring the order API success rate notices that metrics cannot be retrieved during a particular period. Choose one incorrect way to handle this period.
finalQuestions.title: Periods When Metrics Cannot Be Retrieved

choices.text: Define the API operations in scope, the conditions for counting a request as successful, the target value, and the aggregation period.
choices.explanation: This clarifies which results from which operations are counted and which period’s results are compared with the target.

choices.text: Treat calendar months and the most recent 28 days as results from the same range without distinguishing them.
choices.explanation: Calendar months and the most recent 28 days differ in the period and length being evaluated.

choices.text: Issue notifications, but do not decide what the recipient should check.
choices.explanation: Define contacts and verification procedures so that the operator can take action.

choices.text: Define how to handle missing data and what to check after a notification.
choices.explanation: This prevents missed measurement stoppages and helps the operator decide the next action.

choices.text: Determine the success rate using only the number of successful requests without defining the total number of target requests.
choices.explanation: Define the entire number of requests in scope so that the success rate can be calculated.

finalQuestions.prompt: The operations team for the Orders API configures an SLO in CloudWatch that classifies each target request as successful or failed and evaluates the success rate. An alert notifies the team when operator action is required. Select two appropriate actions for this design.
finalQuestions.title: Designing SLOs and alerts

choices.text: Record the occurrence time, target operation, impact on users, and changes made immediately beforehand.
choices.explanation: You can later check logs and metrics under the same conditions.

choices.text: Conclude that a single metric is the cause as soon as it changes at the same time.
choices.explanation: A simultaneous change alone does not show the relationship between cause and effect.

choices.text: Develop candidate causes from the observed data and system configuration.
choices.explanation: This links possible causes with the data to check next.

choices.text: Consider what would be recorded if each candidate were correct, then compare it with logs and traces.
choices.explanation: You can compare candidate causes using evidence.

choices.text: Exclude results that do not fit the initial assessment and do not revisit the candidate causes.
choices.explanation: Results that do not fit the assessment are also material for revising the hypothesis.

finalQuestions.prompt: Intermittent timeouts are occurring in the Orders API. When investigating the cause of the incident, select two incorrect actions.
finalQuestions.title: Testing an incident hypothesis

choices.text: Conclude that user wait time also decreased solely because CPU utilization decreased.
choices.explanation: Measure the time users waited and the error rate to confirm the actual impact.

choices.text: Before and after the change, compare response time and error rate while keeping the target operation, aggregation-period length, and load the same.
choices.explanation: Keeping comparison conditions consistent makes it easier to examine the impact of the change.

choices.text: Compare RDS Proxy’s DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency before and after the change to determine whether the time the proxy takes to obtain a database connection decreased.
choices.explanation: This metric shows in microseconds how long RDS Proxy took to obtain a database connection. Measure the Orders API response time separately.

choices.text: Change the configuration in all environments at once based only on the fact that connection waits and delayed responses occurred simultaneously.
choices.explanation: A simultaneous change alone cannot establish the cause. Testing in some environments limits the impact.

choices.text: Record the conditions of the change, the results, and what is still unknown.
choices.explanation: This allows the basis for the decision to be checked later and the same conditions to be reproduced in a subsequent investigation.

finalQuestions.prompt: The Orders API connects to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL through Amazon RDS Proxy. Order confirmation has become slower, and the operations team suspects the time RDS Proxy takes to lend out a database connection. When changing the connection pool configuration in some environments, select two incorrect ways to verify the effect.
finalQuestions.title: Testing the database connection pool

choices.text: Check the request volume, the status of dependencies, and traces for the relevant operations to narrow down possible causes.
choices.explanation: Comparing multiple data points helps validate possible causes.

choices.text: For the same API operation, compare the error rate and response time before and after the change under equivalent conditions.
choices.explanation: This confirms whether the impact on users has improved.

choices.text: Treat CPU load as the sole cause simply because CPU utilization and 5xx errors increased during the same period.
choices.explanation: Other factors, such as request volume, may have affected both.

choices.text: Test the mitigation in part of the environment and measure whether the change reduces the anomalies.
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to investigate whether the mitigation worked while limiting the impact.

choices.text: Directly compare the SLO attainment rates before and after the change even when the aggregation periods or API operations differ.
choices.explanation: When the periods or operations differ, the requests being evaluated also change, making it difficult to determine whether the difference resulted from the mitigation.

finalQuestions.prompt: The person responsible for the Orders API notices that both the number of HTTP 5xx errors and CPU utilization have increased. Choose two incorrect responses regarding investigating the cause and confirming the effectiveness of the mitigation.
finalQuestions.title: Evaluating CPU load mitigation

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Using an order API as the example, you will learn how to read metrics, investigate the causes of incidents, and verify the effectiveness of countermeasures.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: You will be able to explain how to use metrics, logs, and traces appropriately, as well as service quality objectives and the process for investigating incidents.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Distinguish what can be learned from metrics, logs, and traces.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Examine response time, errors, request volume, and throughput to investigate the impact on users and possible causes.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Decide on metrics, target values, the aggregation period, and the procedure to follow when notified.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Can formulate and test hypotheses about the causes of incidents and compare the impact on users before and after a change.

blocks.label: Find anomalies and trace a single transaction
blocks.text: When the Orders API is slow, first look at the response-time metrics. Metrics are values recorded over time. They can narrow down when the anomaly began and which operation is showing symptoms.

blocks.label: Find anomalies and trace a single transaction
blocks.text: Logs retain errors and request IDs from that time. A trace shows which services a single request passed through and how long each operation took.

blocks.label: Find anomalies and trace a single transaction
blocks.text: First narrow the scope with metrics, then check the logs and traces from the same time period. Keeping the time, request ID, and trace ID traceable makes it easier to correlate different data.

steps.label: Find anomalies and trace a single transaction

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: An order API monitoring operator noticed around noon that the time to complete a purchase had increased.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: They look at response times by operation and confirm that only order registration had become slower.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: They examine the IDs of failed requests and the error details in logs from the same period.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: They open the trace for the slow request and check which call took the most time.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: The process that called the inventory service was taking a long time. The investigation can be narrowed to the inventory service and its dependencies.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: You can determine the cause of one slow request by looking at the API’s overall average response time.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The overall change can be determined from the average response time. To understand the breakdown of one request, examine the trace of the request in question.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Use metrics to narrow down the scope of an anomaly.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Logs show individual events, while traces show the processing path of a single request.

blocks.label: Observe latency, errors, load, and capacity
blocks.text: Looking at a service's state from four perspectives makes it easier to choose where to begin an investigation. Latency represents how long users waited, errors represent failed processing, traffic represents the volume of requests received, and saturation represents how close processing capacity is to its limit.

blocks.label: Observe latency, errors, load, and capacity
blocks.text: Even when average latency does not change, some requests may become significantly slower. p95 is an approximate measure indicating that about 95% of measured requests completed within that time. Compare the same API operation over periods of the same length and using the same units.

blocks.label: Observe latency, errors, load, and capacity
blocks.text: If a queue is growing, processing capacity may be insufficient. You cannot identify the cause merely because CPU utilization and errors increased at the same time. Check the request volume and the state of dependencies, and investigate whether there is another cause.

steps.label: Observe latency, errors, load, and capacity

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The owner of the order API confirmed that latency and HTTP 5xx errors were increasing during the lunch break.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Line up the order-registration p95 latency, error rate, and request count for the same time period.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check not only CPU utilization, but also the number of requests waiting for processing and the wait time for database connections.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Keep the increase in request volume and latency in dependent services as candidate causes, and investigate them using logs and traces.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You will be able to explain separately the impact on users and the candidate causes.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If CPU utilization and the error rate increase at the same time, you can conclude that the CPU is the cause.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: A single change may have affected both. Also investigate the request volume during the same period and the processing time of each service.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Measure the impact on users using latency and errors.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Changes in request volume and saturation are clues for investigating the cause.

blocks.label: Define quality metrics and objectives
blocks.text: A service level indicator (SLI) is a value that measures service quality. For an order API, the percentage of order requests that succeed within 500 milliseconds can be used as a metric. First define the requests to include and the conditions for counting a request as successful.

blocks.label: Define quality metrics and objectives
blocks.text: A service level objective (SLO) is the target you want to achieve for that metric. For example, “At least 99.9% of order requests in the most recent 28 days succeed within 500 milliseconds.” In CloudWatch, a method with a moving evaluation period such as the most recent 28 days is called a rolling interval.

blocks.label: Define quality metrics and objectives
blocks.text: CloudWatch supports SLOs evaluated per request and SLOs evaluated by time interval. In this order API example, each request is evaluated individually. For time-based evaluation, we might examine, for example, how much of a day consisted of one-minute periods that met the standard. The day is the evaluation period, and the minute is the evaluation interval.

blocks.label: Define quality metrics and objectives
blocks.text: Also define the alert notification conditions and the responsible people. If metrics cannot be retrieved, use logs or other observability data to determine whether there were no requests or measurement stopped.

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The operations team for the order API decided to measure how long users are kept waiting when making a purchase.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Count the requests received by the order registration API.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Divide the number of requests that succeeded within 500 milliseconds by the total number of requests included in the count.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Set the target for the most recent 28 days to at least 99.9%, and define the procedure for checking when data does not arrive.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Even if the person responsible changes, anyone can verify that the target was met using the same conditions.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If no metrics are displayed on the monitoring dashboard, there was no incident during that period.

blocks.label: Metrics may not be displayed either when there were no requests or when the measurement mechanism stopped. Check the separately aggregated request count and whether the measurement process is running.
blocks.text: Correction

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: SLI is the value being measured, while SLO is the target you want to achieve for that value.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Specify the aggregation period and operations covered, and define the verification procedure after an alert.

blocks.label: Form hypotheses about causes and measure the effectiveness of countermeasures
blocks.text: When investigating an incident, record when it occurred, which operation caused it, and who was affected. Also check the deployment immediately before the incident and changes in request volume, and separate established facts from candidate causes.

blocks.label: Form hypotheses about causes and measure the effectiveness of countermeasures
blocks.text: Suppose the order API is responding slowly and RDS Proxy's DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency has increased. Assume that there are no available connections in the connection pool, and change the configuration in some environments. By examining how this metric changed, you can test the hypothesis.

blocks.label: Form hypotheses about causes and measure the effectiveness of countermeasures
blocks.text: When evaluating a countermeasure, keep conditions such as the target operation, aggregation period, and load consistent before and after the change. Do not rely only on internal metrics; also compare response time and error rate to verify whether the impact on users improved.

steps.label: Form hypotheses about causes and measure the effectiveness of countermeasures

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The operations team believes that the order API became slow because it was waiting for an available database connection.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Measure connection wait time, response time, and error rate under a similar load.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Change only the connection pool settings in some environments and also observe the load on the database side.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Compare the values and traces before and after the change over aggregation periods of the same length, and record the results and anything you could not determine.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: If connection wait times and user wait times have decreased without worsening the error rate, this provides a basis for deciding whether to expand the configuration change.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If changing the configuration lowers CPU utilization, you can conclude that the impact on users has also improved.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: CPU utilization is a value that indicates the internal state. Compare the time users waited and the proportion of processing that failed under the same conditions.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Test hypotheses within a limited scope.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Compare before and after under the same conditions and confirm whether the experience has improved for users.
